title: SLOs, error budgets and profiling
seriesDescription: Topic-by-topic JEE-style quizzes for the backend and AI-engineering interview roadmap: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code writing, plus multi-correct questions. Language core, concurrency, DSA, web frameworks, data access, databases, messaging, resilience, security, testing, system design, LLM and agent engineering.
description: SLIs, SLOs and error budget arithmetic, burn-rate alerts, and profiling a slow endpoint step by step with traces, thread dumps, JFR, async-profiler, py-spy and cProfile.
source: Google SRE book and workbook (SLOs, alerting on SLOs, multiwindow multi-burn-rate); OpenJDK JFR docs and Red Hat JFR guide; async-profiler README; py-spy README; Python profile docs; HikariCP thread-dump write-ups

questions.prompt: An availability SLO of 99.9% is measured over a rolling 30-day window. How many seconds of full outage does the error budget allow?
questions.explanation: 30 days = 2,592,000 seconds. The budget is 0.1% of that, 2,592 seconds, which is 43.2 minutes.

questions.prompt: Match each availability SLO to the downtime it allows over a 30-day window (43,200 minutes).
questions.explanation: Budget = (1 - SLO) x 43,200 minutes. Each extra nine divides the budget by ten, which is why four nines is a very different engineering commitment from three.

questions.prompt: Your SLO is 99.9% of requests succeed. In the last hour 0.4% of requests failed. What is the burn rate (budget consumed relative to the sustainable pace)?
questions.explanation: Allowed error ratio is 0.1%. Observed 0.4% divided by 0.1% is a burn rate of 4: at this pace the 30-day budget is gone in 7.5 days.

questions.prompt: The Google SRE workbook example pages when the burn rate is at least 14.4 over 1 hour (and over 5 minutes). Why 14.4?

options.text: At that rate 2% of a 30-day budget is spent in one hour
It is the 99.9% SLO value rewritten as a multiplier for the alert
options.why: The SLO value does not produce 14.4.

options.text: It equals 24 hours divided by the 1.67 hour page window
options.why: No such relationship is used; the number comes from budget fractions.

options.text: It is an arbitrary vendor default with no maths behind it
options.why: It is derived: pick the budget fraction you refuse to lose, then solve for the rate.

questions.explanation: The short second window (5 minutes) makes the alert reset quickly after the problem is fixed. Pair it with slower, lower-rate tickets (for example burn 1 over 3 days).

questions.prompt: An endpoint receives 200 requests per second and each request holds one DB connection for 250 ms on average. By Little's law, how many connections are in use on average?
questions.explanation: L = lambda x W = 200 x 0.25 = 50. Size the pool with headroom above this, and remember that a slowdown raises W and therefore exhausts the pool.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion and the reason, then choose the option that describes them correctly.
questions.assertion: Page on user-visible symptoms such as SLO burn rather than on causes such as high CPU.
questions.reason: Users only experience failures and latency, and a CPU spike may be harmless.

whys.a: Right: the reason is why symptom alerts have fewer false pages.
whys.b: The reason directly justifies the assertion.

questions.explanation: Cause metrics are still useful on dashboards for diagnosis, just not as the main paging signal.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion and the reason, then choose the option that describes them correctly.
questions.assertion: A team with plenty of unspent error budget can ship riskier changes faster.
questions.reason: The error budget equals one minus the SLO target.

whys.a: The formula does not itself explain the policy of shipping faster.
whys.b: Right: both are true; the policy comes from agreeing that budget is for spending, not from the formula.

questions.explanation: The budget turns reliability into a shared currency between product and operations.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion and the reason, then choose the option that describes them correctly.
questions.assertion: Java Flight Recorder is suitable for continuous recording in production.
questions.reason: JFR rewrites every method with bytecode instrumentation that adds an enter and exit probe.

whys.b: The reason is false, so it cannot be an unrelated truth.
whys.c: Right: JFR is built into the JVM and uses low-overhead event sampling, not bytecode weaving.
whys.d: The assertion is the true one.

questions.explanation: The default configuration (default.jfc) targets roughly 1% overhead or less, which is why it can stay on in production; the heavier profile settings cost more.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion and the reason, then choose the option that describes them correctly.
questions.assertion: A 100% availability SLO is the safest target for a customer-facing API.
questions.reason: Every dependency (network, cloud zone, deploys) can fail, so zero downtime cannot be promised.

whys.d: Right: the assertion is false because it forbids any change, and the reason is true.

questions.explanation: A 100% target leaves no budget for deploys and costs far more than users can perceive.

questions.text: In a flame graph the {1} of a frame shows its share of samples, and stack depth runs along the {2} axis.
questions.explanation: Colours are usually arbitrary; the horizontal order is alphabetical, not time.

questions.prompt: GET /reports is slow only in production. What is the best first step?

options.text: Look at a trace of a slow request to see which span dominates
options.why: Right: locate the slow stage before choosing a profiler.

options.text: Rewrite the whole service logic in a faster language straight away
options.why: A rewrite without a measurement is a guess.

options.text: Double the pod count and see whether it helps
options.why: Scaling hides a lock or database problem and costs money.

options.text: Turn on DEBUG logging for the entire cluster
options.why: It adds load and rarely isolates the slow stage.

questions.explanation: Measure, narrow to a stage (DB, remote call, CPU, lock wait), then use the matching tool: EXPLAIN for SQL, a profiler for CPU, thread dumps for waiting.

questions.prompt: You take three jstack thread dumps ten seconds apart. Which findings point to a connection-pool or lock bottleneck? Select all that apply.

options.text: Many http-nio threads parked (WAITING or TIMED_WAITING) in HikariPool.getConnection in every dump
options.why: Right: threads are queued for a connection.

options.text: Many threads BLOCKED waiting for the same monitor held by one thread
options.why: Right: classic lock contention.

options.text: One thread RUNNABLE in a socket read in a single dump only
options.why: One sample in one dump proves nothing about a bottleneck.

options.text: A thread named Reference Handler WAITING in all dumps
options.why: It is a normal JVM housekeeping thread.

questions.explanation: Repeat the dump: a pattern that persists across samples is signal; a single frame is noise.

questions.prompt: Write the shell command that starts a 60 second Java Flight Recorder recording on the running JVM with pid 4321 and saves it to /tmp/slow.jfr.
questions.explanation: Open the file in JDK Mission Control or run jfr print --events jdk.ExecutionSample. Starting JFR with -XX:StartFlightRecording at launch is the other route, but this question asks about a running process.

questions.prompt: Write the shell command that records a 30 second flame graph of the running Python process 4321 to flame.svg with py-spy, without restarting it.
questions.explanation: py-spy is a sampling profiler that reads the process memory, so it needs ptrace permission (often root). py-spy dump --pid prints the current stacks, like a thread dump.

questions.prompt: Write Python that profiles a call to handle() with cProfile and prints the results sorted by cumulative time.
questions.explanation: pstats.Stats(profile).sort_stats("cumulative").print_stats(20) also works. cProfile traces every call, so overhead is higher than py-spy sampling; use it in dev or on a copy of the workload.

questions.prompt: p99 latency is 5 s but CPU sits at 15% and p50 is fine. A CPU profile shows nothing hot. What kind of problem do you suspect?

options.text: Time spent waiting off CPU: locks, pool queues, I/O or GC pauses
options.why: Right: a CPU profile cannot see waiting; use wall-clock mode or thread dumps.

options.text: A tight loop in business code burning cores
options.why: That would raise CPU usage, which is low.

options.text: A too-small JSON payload
options.why: Small payloads are not a cause of multi-second tails.

options.text: An overly verbose class name in stack traces
options.why: Naming has no effect on latency.

questions.explanation: Off-CPU time is invisible to a CPU profile. async-profiler with -e wall (wall-clock sampling) or -e lock, plus repeated thread dumps, expose waiting; a saturated connection-pool queue is a frequent culprit.

questions.prompt: The SLO is 99.9 percent over 30 days (720 hours). The error ratio runs at a burn rate of 6 for 6 hours. What percentage of the 30-day error budget has been consumed?
questions.explanation: Budget consumed = burn rate x window / period = 6 x 6 / 720 = 0.05, i.e. 5 percent. This is the SRE workbook's second paging tier (6x over 6 hours).

questions.prompt: Match each multiwindow burn-rate alert from the Google SRE workbook example (30-day SLO) with the share of the error budget it represents and the response.

right.text: 2 percent of the budget, page someone
5 percent of the budget, page someone
10 percent of the budget, open a ticket

questions.explanation: Each row is budget consumed = burn rate x window / 720 h: 14.4 x 1/720 = 2%, 6 x 6/720 = 5%, 1 x 72/720 = 10%. Fast burns page, slow burns file a ticket.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a well-formed service level indicator (SLI) for an API?

options.text: Good events over valid events, such as fast non-5xx responses.
options.why: Correct: SLIs are a ratio of good to valid events, so they map directly onto an SLO percentage and an error budget.

options.text: Average CPU utilisation measured across the whole fleet of servers at once.
options.why: A cause or capacity metric; users do not experience CPU.

options.text: The number of pods that are currently running in the production cluster.
options.why: Infrastructure state, not a user-facing proportion.

options.text: Mean time between production deployments, measured over the last quarter.
options.why: A delivery-speed metric, not a measure of service quality as users see it.

questions.explanation: Pick the measurement point (load balancer or client), define 'good' (status and latency threshold) and 'valid' (exclude health checks and caller errors), then set the SLO target on that ratio.
